title: Probabilistic predictions for partial least squares using bootstrap
contribution: A bootstrap-by-pairs predictive distribution for standard NIPALS PLS that captures latent-space uncertainty, applied to Design Space identification and prediction intervals for Eli Lilly process data.
problem_entry: Practitioners' PLS has hard-to-model prediction uncertainty because data affect the latent space nonlinearly; the 1980s-90s linearised (zeroth-order, student-t) estimators were compute-era approximations, and bootstrap by residuals ignores input variation (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: Resample (x,y) pairs, rerun unchanged NIPALS on each resample with its MLE noise variance, and average the B Gaussians; input-dependent spread comes from the bootstrap means (eqs. 15-21, Algorithm 1, pp. 4-6).
assumptions: Normally distributed prediction error, PLS a reasonable model, training data drawn like future data (p. 2); no result known that PLS parameters are a joint MLE (p. 4); Design Space problems may not follow PLS latent structure (p. 7).
proof_devices: bootstrap predictive distribution as an expectation over bootstrap data sets from the empirical distribution, Monte Carlo approximated, eqs. 17-19 (pp. 4-5)
Design Space probability by a normal c.d.f. difference (eq. 23) or Monte Carlo sampling (Algorithm 2) (p. 6)
experiments: Five case studies vs the zeroth-order method (synthetic with true Design Space, Michael addition, industrial reductive amination, wet granulation leave-one-out, confidential spectroscopy); visual comparisons, tie on spectroscopy reported (pp. 5-11).
positioning: Builds on Denham (bootstrap by residuals) and Fushiki (bootstrap predictive distributions); older methods framed as compute-era approximations, probabilistic PLS rejected for abandoning NIPALS (pp. 2-4).
writing: Claim scoped up front to low-data, non-standard-linear settings (p. 5); uncertainty about real-case accuracy admitted (p. 9).
limits_future: Assumes linear model plus noise and cannot separate noise from model-mismatch uncertainty; future: model-mismatch uncertainty, experimental spaces, Real Time Release Testing (p. 12).

method_links.note: Keeps the partner's trusted model (PLS/NIPALS, 'speed, familiarity') and wraps uncertainty around it instead of encoding it as constraints.
One widely used baseline, ground truth only where computable, tie written in; no coverage metric and no second competitor run (Denham discussed only).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: wrap uncertainty around the practitioner's standard estimator rather than replace it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: NIPALS kept unchanged; probabilistic PLS rejected because it 'does not provide the same solution as the standard NIPALS algorithm'; bootstrap by pairs reruns NIPALS per resample.

transferable: Validate an uncertainty method first where the true answer is computable (synthetic generator with a true Design Space), then on real data by held-out coverage (pp. 7-11).
Include a case where the incumbent is known to work well and report the tie, showing no loss where the old method is trusted (p. 11).
coauthors: James Odgers, Chrysoula Kappatou, Salvador García Muñoz (Eli Lilly), Sarah Filippi (corresponding); Misener 3rd of 5

quotes.text: The novelty of our method is in how to weight different sets of PLS parameters according to how well they describe the data.
One point which we would like to acknowledge is that Design Space identification problems often do not follow the latent structure implicitly assumed by PLS.

title: Data augmentation driven by optimization for membrane separation process synthesis
contribution: ADORO, a data-augmentation scheme that densifies an ANN surrogate's training data around multistart stationary points where surrogate and simulator disagree, giving membrane designs as good as a 343k-point model with at most 50k points.
problem_entry: An ANN surrogate embedded in the membrane-design NLP avoids discretised-ODE trouble, but optimisation drives decisions into regions where the ANN is inaccurate, and a dense 343k data set costs more than 5 days to fit (pp. 1-5).
key_idea: Grade and refine the surrogate where the optimiser goes: simulate all multistart stationary points over several purity/recovery scenarios, keep those with discrepancy above epsilon, perturb around them and retrain (S1-S4, eq. 2, pp. 9-10); baseline is gradient-direction adversarial augmentation (eq. 1, p. 7).
assumptions: Three-input, two-output single-membrane ANN (one sigmoid hidden layer to keep NLP constraints simple) trained on MEMSIC data; SVM hyperplane of simulator failures imposed as a constraint; two-stage CO2/H2 case at 90/95/99% purity (pp. 3-5).
proof_devices: linear SVM boundary of simulator-failure region used as an optimisation constraint (pp. 3-4)
discrepancy-filtered perturbation around stationary points, eq. 2 (p. 10)
experiments: Every best design re-simulated in MEMSIC; simulated purity and flow errors for sampling schemes, data-set sizes, AAD and ADORO (Tables 1, 4, 5, 7, pp. 5-10); normalised design cost (p. 11); total time including model building vs discretisation baseline (Table 9, p. 13); no seed repetitions.
positioning: Against ML adversarial augmentation and PSE sampling-based surrogate work; related in the conclusion to batch and multi-fidelity BO including SnAKe (pp. 2-3, 13).
writing: Introduction (Misener's per CRediT) opens with the decision problem; a box-plot vs feasibility contradiction is explained rather than hidden (pp. 1, 7, 13).
limits_future: Single case study, one augmentation iteration, 50k-start ADORO runs omitted as disappointing, data not shareable; future: reuse augmented data across purity levels (pp. 10, 13).

method_links.note: Trained ANN inserted as equality constraints in the NLP, architecture chosen for the optimisation model; SVM failure boundary as a learned trust-region variant of step 4.
Surrogates graded by the simulated feasibility and cost of the optimiser's final design, not training error; authors show the two disagree.
Every returned design re-checked by simulator, over- vs under-estimation separated, timings include model building, failed 50k ADORO runs reported as omitted.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Densify surrogate training data at multistart stationary points where surrogate and simulator disagree, across several requirement scenarios, rather than everywhere or only at the global optimum.

transferable: Grade a surrogate by re-simulating the optimiser's answer and report over- and under-estimation separately, since one gives infeasible and the other expensive designs (pp. 3, 5).
Learn the simulator's failure region with a simple classifier and impose its boundary as a constraint so the optimiser cannot exploit meaningless regions (pp. 3-4).
Augment around all multistart stationary points across scenarios, not just the global optimum, which yields too few and non-robust points (p. 3).
coauthors: Bernardetta Addis (corresponding), Christophe Castel, Amalia Macali, Veronica Piccialli; Misener 4th of 5, wrote introduction and literature review (CRediT, p. 13)

quotes.text: The core idea is that the model accuracy must be high not everywhere, but only around some regions of interest, namely, the regions around the local optimum points.
focusing only on the global minimum point over the entire decision-making problem is therefore not enough to us

title: Practical path-based Bayesian optimization
contribution: Three practical extensions of SnAKe path-based BO (self-stopping with an uncertainty guard, truncation for maximum input change, random-scalarisation multi-objective) with synthetic and SnAr benchmarks.
problem_entry: Entered from the group's own method's limits: SnAKe needs a fixed budget, allows unbounded single moves, and handles one objective (numbered I-III, p. 2).
key_idea: Minimal modifications of SnAKe: EI-per-cost point deletion guarded by posterior variance (Algorithm 1, p. 3), step truncation to deltaMAX (Algorithm 2, p. 4), random-scalarisation Thompson sampling for the batch (Algorithm 3, p. 4); TSP ordering kept.
assumptions: Cost = fixed experiment cost + input-change cost (eq. 2, p. 3); rate-of-change constraint emulated by a jump cost (p. 5); independent GPs per objective (p. 4).
experiments: Branin2D, Hartmann3D/6D, Shekel and SnAr; 25 runs, ±0.5 std bands, average budget used reported; strengthened baseline EIpu+Std; NSGA-II reference Pareto front; losses to TrEI and EIpu+Std reported (pp. 4-6, 10-12).
positioning: Within path-based BO (Ramesh, Mutny, MONGOOSE, Paulson); restores SnAr's original multi-objective form (pp. 2, 5).
writing: Short paper with one subsection per numbered limitation; conclusion limited to empirical advantages (pp. 2-6).
limits_future: No selection rule for thresholds delta and nu, synthetic benchmarks, narrow error bands; code promised after peer review (pp. 3-5, 10).

method_links.note: Step 8, re-grade your own earlier work: opens by listing SnAKe's practical limits and its high cost for small gains.
Step 3, strengthen the baseline: authors boost EIpu with their own variance criterion; losses written in. Scale is light (synthetic, ±0.5 std, no test).
New thresholds delta, nu and deltaMAX introduced without a robustness sweep; only robustness to the maximum budget shown.

transferable: Add a model-uncertainty guard to any BO stopping rule and show the vanilla rule stopping too early (Algorithm 1, p. 3; Fig. 1, p. 5).
Report average budget used next to regret and rerun with a larger cap to show the self-stopping spend does not scale with it (p. 5).
When a baseline wins a metric for a structural reason, show the metric's sensitivity with a relaxed definition rather than dropping it (p. 10).
coauthors: Jose Pablo Folch (first), James Odgers, Shiqiang Zhang, Robert M Lee, Behrang Shafei, David Walz (BASF), Calvin Tsay, Mark van der Wilk; Misener last of 9

quotes.text: SnAKe is limited in some practical aspects.
Vanilla EIpu stops too early due to model misspecification; our modification that includes uncertainty criteria greatly improves performance.

title: Gaussian processes for monitoring air-quality in Kampala
contribution: An empirical study of GP kernels, outlier removal, weather inputs and sparse approximations for PM2.5 nowcasting and forecasting on AirQo's 66-sensor Kampala network.
problem_entry: Sparse low-cost sensor networks in low- and middle-income cities need data-efficient models with uncertainty; prior GP studies used unavailable pollutant inputs and only forecast (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Stack modelling choices one at a time (periodic temporal kernel, training-outlier removal, weather inputs, SVGP/ST-SVGP) and evaluate on nowcasting (leave-one-site-out) and forecasting (last day held out) (pp. 3-4, 7-8).
assumptions: Gaussian-noise GP regression; one month of calibrated hourly data from 66 sites; citywide weather from one station; non-sparse models on 1000 random points, 4 repeats (pp. 2-3, 7-8).
experiments: Cumulative Tables 1-2 with min/average/max RMSE across sites; test outliers kept; negative results reported for weather inputs and ST-SVGP forecasting (p. 4).
positioning: Against Reggente, Jang and Cheng GP air-quality studies, differentiated by available inputs and the nowcasting task (p. 2).
writing: Short empirical note; conclusion names a non-stationary kernel and sensor placement as next steps (p. 4).
limits_future: One month of data, single weather station, similar worst-site nowcasting error suggesting more sensors or non-stationary kernels needed (pp. 4, 8).

method_links.note: Cumulative ablation design (step 2) applied to a prediction pipeline instead of inside a B&B.
Test outliers kept for fair comparison, worst-site error reported, negative results written in.

transferable: Clean only the training set, leave test outliers in place and say so, so the error does not flatter the cleaning step (pp. 4, 8).
Report worst-site (max) RMSE next to the average to show where the model fails and motivate more sensors or non-stationary kernels (p. 4).
coauthors: Clara Stoddart, Lauren Shrack, Richard Sserunjogi, Usman Abdul-Ganiy, Engineer Bainomugisha, Deo Okure (AirQo), Jose Pablo Folch and Ruby Sedgwick (equal contribution); Misener 7th of 9

quotes.text: We do not remove outliers from the test set for fair comparison.
The additional variables don’t seem to lead to any clear improvement in model performance.
